title: How Excessive Screen Time Is Fueling India's Lifestyle Disease Crisis
excerpt: Rising screen use across all age groups is contributing to obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular risks in India, where over 54% of adults are already physically inactive.
body:
• Indians now spend an average of 3-4 hours daily on screens, contributing to sedentary lifestyles that are driving a surge in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular disease
  • The ICMR-INDIAB study found that 54.4% of Indian adults over 20 are physically inactive, rising to 65% in urban areas — with over 90% doing no recreational exercise at all
  • Around 90 million Indians are diabetic and 136 million are pre-diabetic, with doctors reporting that 90% of diabetes cases are lifestyle-related

A Growing Health Emergency

India is staring at a lifestyle disease crisis driven in part by a factor most people barely think about: screen time. As smartphones, tablets, and laptops become central to work, education, and entertainment, the hours Indians spend sedentary in front of screens are climbing — and so are rates of diabetes, obesity, and heart disease.

According to doctors at Yatharth Hospital in Delhi-NCR, screen exposure has risen sharply across all age groups, from children to the elderly. With entertainment, gaming, and social activities increasingly happening on phones, people are averaging three to four hours of daily screen time. This sedentary behavior increases body fat, leading to obesity, insulin resistance, and a higher risk of diabetes, as reported by SugerMint.

The Numbers Paint a Stark Picture

The scale of India's inactivity problem is staggering. The ICMR-INDIAB study, one of the country's largest diabetes surveys, found that 54.4% of Indian adults over 20 are physically inactive. In urban areas, that figure rises to 65%. Over 90% of Indians engage in no recreational exercise at all, according to OnlyMyHealth.

India now has approximately 90 million people living with diabetes and another 136 million who are pre-diabetic, according to medical data cited by hospital experts. Dr. Rajeev Gupta, Senior Director of Internal Medicine at Yatharth Hospital, stated that roughly 90% of diabetes cases are lifestyle-related.

"Prolonged screen exposure, lack of exercise, and poor diet weaken insulin efficiency. Even children are now showing early signs of insulin resistance when their screen time exceeds three to four hours daily."

— Dr. Rajeev Gupta, Senior Director, Internal Medicine, Yatharth Hospital

Children and Young Adults at Risk

The concern is not limited to middle-aged adults. A cross-sectional study of 3,920 students aged 6-19 in urban schools in Pune found that screen time was significantly linked to higher rates of overweight and obesity, according to research published in Frontiers in Public Health. A separate study in Tamil Nadu found that 73% of children under 5 had excessive screen time, with strong associations with developmental delays, particularly in language acquisition, as reported in PLOS ONE.

Dr. Sanjay Gupta, also at Yatharth Hospital, highlighted that Type 2 diabetes is now emerging in individuals under 25. A study found 12.3% prevalence of diabetes indicators among adolescent boys and 8.4% among girls. Many Indians, despite being lean, carry high internal visceral fat that makes them prone to diabetes-related complications, he added.

The Biological Mechanism

When people spend prolonged periods sitting, muscle activity — especially in the lower body — drops significantly. This impairs glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity. Over time, the body develops insulin resistance, accumulates abdominal fat, and mounts an increased inflammatory response, all of which directly contribute to diabetes, according to research published in Discover Public Health by Springer Nature.

Screen time before bed compounds the problem. Research published in The Lancet Regional Health showed that nighttime light exposure from screens disrupts the body's internal clock, keeps the nervous system in an alert state, raises stress hormones, and can elevate blood sugar levels, according to Livemint.

The Diaspora Dimension

For Indians living abroad, the same risks apply — often amplified by desk-bound tech jobs and long commutes. The genetic predisposition to insulin resistance and visceral fat accumulation that many South Asians carry makes screen-driven sedentary lifestyles particularly dangerous for the diaspora, where diabetes rates already run significantly higher than the general population in countries like the United States and the United Kingdom.

What Experts Recommend

Medical experts recommend limiting recreational screen time, incorporating at least 30-45 minutes of daily exercise, taking walking breaks every hour during desk work, and avoiding screen use before bed. Regular blood sugar screenings are strongly advised, particularly for those with sedentary occupations. As Dr. Ritesh Kumar Chaudhary, a consultant diabetologist, told OnlyMyHealth: "Every bit of movement helps the body use insulin better, which is why even simple, everyday activity makes a huge difference in preventing diabetes."
